WITH due AS (
  SELECT id
  FROM topics
  WHERE enabled
    AND next_run_at <= now()
  ORDER BY next_run_at
  LIMIT __ENVVAR:AR_DISPATCH_BATCH_CAP__
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
-- Claim and reschedule are one statement on purpose. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED holds a
-- claimed row for exactly as long as the transaction that took it, so a claim
-- committed before next_run_at moves leaves the row unlocked and still due, which
-- invites the following tick to run it again. Lifting this UPDATE out into a second
-- node or a second statement is that mistake, and it reads as tidying. Run over one
-- set of due rows twice, the folded form takes them on the first pass and nothing on
-- the second. A claim that only SELECTed hands back the same ids both times.

-- LEAST and GREATEST ignore a NULL argument, so a bound the row does not carry is
-- skipped rather than stood in with COALESCE, which would cap a floored interval back
-- to the proposal and leave the floor doing nothing. clampIntervalSeconds in
-- src/lib/schedule.ts is this same rule as TypeScript, and argues both in full.
UPDATE topics AS t
SET next_run_at = now() + make_interval(secs => LEAST(
  t.max_interval_seconds,
  GREATEST(t.min_interval_seconds, t.interval_seconds)
))
FROM due
WHERE t.id = due.id
-- Five columns because this projection is the shape the merged claim stream carries:
-- every branch answers in it, so the nodes past the merge read one item kind rather
-- than one per table. unit_kind is a literal because nothing in a claimed row says
-- which table it came from, and once the branches merge that is the only thing left
-- to route on. RETURNING on an UPDATE reads the row as written, so next_run_at is
-- the time this pass set rather than the one that made the row due.
RETURNING
  t.id,
  t.domain_id,
  'topic'::text AS unit_kind,
  t.name,
  t.next_run_at

WITH due AS (
  SELECT id
  FROM export_subscriptions
  WHERE enabled
    AND next_run_at <= now()
  ORDER BY next_run_at
  LIMIT __ENVVAR:AR_DISPATCH_BATCH_CAP__
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
-- The same statement as Claim Due Topics, against the other schedulable table. One
-- dispatcher reads both the same way, so the two arguments that shape it are written
-- out on that node and are not repeated here: why the claim and the reschedule are
-- folded into one statement, and why the clamp skips a null bound rather than
-- standing it in with COALESCE. What differs is the table, and the projection below.

-- This claim sits beside Claim Due Topics off the Schedule Trigger rather than behind
-- it, and the difference is a multiplication rather than a preference. A Postgres
-- node runs its statement once per INPUT item, mapping the query over every item it
-- was handed, so chained behind that claim this one would run once per claimed topic,
-- each run taking a fresh batch off this table and rescheduling every row in it. Its
-- run count would be settled by what the node in front emitted, a fact about the
-- other table that says nothing about this one. What makes the parallel form run once
-- is the other half: the trigger emits a single item per fire. Neither half implies
-- the other, and without the emit count a branch off the trigger could multiply for
-- the same reason a chained one does.

-- The cap is per claim and not per tick. This LIMIT and the one on Claim Due Topics
-- read one setting, so a tick finding both tables backlogged claims up to twice it,
-- and both claims have already moved next_run_at on every row they took. So the
-- second application of the cap, over the merged stream, is a choice about which
-- claimed rows are RUN and not a re-check of a batch already inside the cap. What it
-- leaves behind was rescheduled without being dispatched, and comes round again a
-- whole interval later. capBatch in src/lib/schedule.ts carries the rest of that
-- argument.
UPDATE export_subscriptions AS s
SET next_run_at = now() + make_interval(secs => LEAST(
  s.max_interval_seconds,
  GREATEST(s.min_interval_seconds, s.interval_seconds)
))
FROM due
WHERE s.id = due.id
-- The five columns Claim Due Topics answers in, plus one of this branch's own.
-- export_subscriptions carries no name, so the label is the format, which is what the
-- row renders. It does not identify the row: a domain may take one format at two
-- destinations, and connector_id is what tells those apart. That column rides on this
-- branch alone, so nothing past the merge may read one off an arbitrary claimed unit.
-- unit_kind is 'export' rather than this table's own singular because it names the
-- dispatch the row asks for, and pairs with AR_EXPORT_WORKFLOW_ID the way 'topic'
-- pairs with AR_TOPIC_WORKFLOW_ID.
RETURNING
  s.id,
  s.domain_id,
  'export'::text AS unit_kind,
  s.format AS name,
  s.next_run_at,
  s.connector_id

nodes.name: Merge Claims
nodes.notes: Append, so what leaves here is the two claim branches concatenated: nothing is dropped, added or rewritten, and a table with nothing due never holds the tick, append needing data from only one input to continue. What it does not pass on is which branch an item came in on, which is what unit_kind stands in for downstream. A tick claiming nothing does not arrive as nothing: a Postgres node whose statement is not a SELECT emits one success item when it returns no rows, so an empty tick reaches here as two items carrying no unit_kind. Dropping them belongs to the Code node, keyed on the absent unit_kind rather than on a branch.

## Build Stamp

**__ENVVAR:AR_BUILD_TAG__**

The git short commit `scripts/build-workflows.ts` resolved when it wrote this artifact. A stamp that does not match the commit you deployed means the instance is running an older import.

`dev` is a build with no commit to name, and a `-dirty` suffix a tree carrying uncommitted changes. Neither is an older import.
